constitutive_assumptions: Plane stress assumption of classical laminated plate theory (transverse shear stresses XZ, YZ and transverse normal stress ZZ neglected)
Linear elastic behavior for the constraining layer and fluidic layer with plane stress-reduced stiffnesses
Nonlinear constitutive stress function for the 90-degree elastomeric matrix composite (EMC) modeled by a fourth-order (quartic) polynomial derived from uniaxial tensile test data
Thin-plate assumption with uniform thickness for the constraining layer (strain energy of ribs assumed negligible in thin regions)
Memoryless pneumatic pressurization system with zero initial pressure (P0 = 0)
Adiabatic expansion process of air with adiabatic coefficient gamma = 1.4
Small rotation and deflection within each local segment coordinate frame (slope derivative less than 1, segment rotation angle beta_i < 45 degrees)
control_variables: Actuator total length (Lx = 120 mm), width (Ly = 35 mm), and total height (H = 9.4 mm)
Out-of-plane lamina heights with respect to midplane (h1, h2, h3, h3b)
Fluidic rib dimensions (transverse rib width w1 = 2 mm, rib thickness t = 2 mm, rib spacing w2 = 6 mm)
Elastomer material (Bluestar Bluesil V-340/CA 45 silicone rubber)
Fiber reinforcement type (3-K bidirectional woven carbon fiber fabric with 0-degree fibers removed)
Prescribed deflection during force measurement (10 mm)
dependent_variables: Actuator midplane equilibrium shape and coordinates (u0_Ne, w0_Ne)
Flexural rigidity along the X-axis (Kx) and Z-axis (Kz)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Discretizing a fluidic prestressed composite actuator into chained local elements modeled via low-order displacement polynomials and Rayleigh-Ritz energy minimization enables accurate computation of large deflections and non-constant curvatures in several seconds.

Replacing a rigid metal inlet tube with an oversized compressed soft PVC tube inside the molded channel increased the maximum leak-free operating pneumatic pressure from 80 kPa to approximately 400 kPa.

Integrating longitudinal and transverse elastomeric ribs within the internal fluid channel suppresses out-of-plane ballooning under high pneumatic pressure and effectively translates fluid pressure into an unbending moment.

Increasing prestrain in the bottom elastomeric matrix composite layer increases unactuated equilibrium curvature and grasping-direction flexural rigidity, while requiring higher actuation pressure to completely flatten.
Increasing the internal fluid channel width and upper height increases unactuated curvature, reduces flexural rigidity, and decreases the pneumatic pressure required to achieve flattening.

Optical motion capture tests using reflective markers confirmed that measured quasi-static actuator profiles and curvatures across prestrains of 0.15, 0.25, and 0.40 closely match chained composite model (CCM8) predictions.

Tip-loading bending tests showed flexural rigidity along the grasping direction decreases with increasing pressure, agreeing well with CCM8 predictions at 0.40 prestrain, whereas Z-axis modeled rigidity overpredicts compliance due to unmodeled constraining ribs and plane stress assumptions.
A prototype three-finger soft gripper demonstrated passive grasping of various object geometries at zero pressure and opened upon simultaneous pressurization.

experimental_setup: Elastomeric elements fabricated from Bluestar Bluesil V-340/CA 45 silicone rubber (Shore 45A hardness)
90-degree EMC fabricated by removing longitudinal fibers from 3-K bidirectional woven carbon fiber fabric and sandwiching between cured silicone layers
3D-printed PLA molds (Ultimaker S5) and sacrificial paraffin wax cores cast in water-soluble 3D-printed PVA molds to produce internal channel ribs
Polypropylene (PP) constraining layer 3D-printed with transverse stiffening ribs
Layer bonding using silicone sealant (DAP Auto-Marine 100% RTV) and cyanoacrylate (Loctite 681925)
Pressurization interface using soft PVC tubing (3.2 mm OD) press-fitted into a 1.65 mm molded channel
Motion capture system using four OptiTrack cameras (1.3 MP resolution) tracking reflective markers along the actuator midplane
Pneumatic regulation setup using a laboratory compressed air line, pressure regulator, and pressure gauge
Bending and stiffness measurement using a Mark-10 ES20 load frame with a Mark-10 ME-200 force gauge connected via fishing line to a 3D-printed end fixture
Demonstration soft gripper constructed with three composite actuator fingers mounted on a 3D-printed PLA palm
future_work: Design and modeling of gripper integration and multi-finger grasping capability using analytical models
Developing smart soft grippers with embedded sensors to enable precise closed-loop control
Incorporating advanced plate theories (first-order or third-order shear deformation plate theories) to account for transverse stresses
Incorporating the constraining layer ribs directly into the analytical mechanical model
independent_variables: Applied pneumatic pressure (0 to ~400 kPa; 0 to 82.7 kPa in loading experiments)
Applied tip forces (f0 in X-direction, p0 in Z-direction) / tip displacement (10 mm)
Internal fluid channel width (Cy) and upper height (h3a)
limitations_inferred: The analytical model and experiments consider only quasi-static behavior, ignoring dynamic effects, viscoelastic relaxation, and rate-dependent hysteresis of silicone rubber.
The energy formulation assumes ideal adiabatic air expansion and a memoryless state from zero pressure, which may not hold under rapid cyclic actuation.
Only simplified point loads at the free end were modeled and measured; distributed contact forces, friction, and lateral torsion during multi-finger grasping were not captured.
Evaluation of the multi-finger gripper was qualitative; payload limits, maximum grip forces, and object retention under disturbance were not quantified.
Multi-step fabrication involving sacrificial wax melting and manual adhesive layer alignment presents repeatability and manufacturing tolerance constraints.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The plane stress assumption neglects transverse shear and normal stresses, which underpredicts bending forces.

Internal channel ribs (2 mm x 2 mm) violate the small thickness assumption of classical plate theory (thickness no greater than one-tenth of in-plane dimensions), reducing curvature and bending flexibility.
The thick ribs (4 mm) of the constraining layer could not be modeled in the CCM due to violation of the plane stress assumption, causing the model to underestimate actuator stiffness.
Internal rib deformation consumes a proportionally larger amount of net energy at low prestrain (0.15), contributing to divergence in curvature-pressure slopes.
Circle fitting RMSD increases with pressure because the unactuated tip region lacks an internal fluid channel and does not deform under pressure.
Motion capture precision was affected by using only seven discrete markers and manual marker alignment imperfections.
Dimensional variability in experimental composite prototypes contributed to divergence from model predictions.
main_results: The chained composite model converges with increasing segment number, with eight segments (CCM8) providing a converged trade-off between accuracy and low computational time (~3.8 s).
Replacing rigid inlet tubes with an oversized compressed soft PVC tube increased maximum burst/leakage pressure from 80 kPa to ~400 kPa, enabling larger initial curvatures and strokes.
Internal longitudinal and transverse ribs effectively prevented out-of-plane ballooning and translated fluid pressure into actuator flattening.
Precurved composite actuators hold passive grasping posture without energy expenditure; pneumatic pressurization straightens the fingers, decreasing flexural rigidity toward zero.
Higher prestrains produce higher unactuated curvature and larger flexural rigidity, requiring higher pressure to achieve full flattening.
Larger fluid channel width and height produce higher unactuated curvature and lower flexural rigidity, reducing actuation pressure needed for opening.
Optical motion capture validated that measured actuator midplane curvatures across prestrains of 0.15, 0.25, and 0.40 agreed well with CCM8 predictions.

Bending tests demonstrated that flexural rigidity along the grasping direction decreases with pressure, matching CCM8 calculations closely for 0.40 prestrain, with moderate divergence for 0.25 prestrain and softer-than-actual predictions along the Z-axis due to plane stress and rib omissions.
A three-finger soft robotic gripper prototype successfully grasped objects of diverse shapes upon pressure release.
modeling_methods: Chained composite model (CCM) segmenting the actuator into discrete elements along its longitudinal axis
Small rotation model (SRM) formulated for each segment in its local moving coordinate frame
Lagrangian strain formulation accounting for geometric nonlinearity
Third-order displacement polynomial shape functions with unknown coefficients for midplane displacements
Variational Rayleigh-Ritz method minimizing total net potential energy (strain energy minus work of fluid pressure and external forces)
Newton-Raphson numerical algorithm solving the resulting 4N nonlinear algebraic equations
Least-squares circle fitting to calculate effective curvatures and root-mean-square deviations (RMSD)
performance_metrics: Flexural rigidity along the X and Z axes (Kx, Kz in N*m^2)
Tip reaction force (N) at 10 mm displacement
Root-mean-square deviation of circle fitting (RMSD in mm)
possible_gap_implications: Classical laminated plate theory underpredicts bending forces and cannot capture thick stiffening ribs, indicating a research gap for higher-order shear deformation plate theories (FSDT/TSDT) or 3D continuum formulations in ribbed composite soft actuators.
Neglecting rate-dependent viscoelasticity points to an open problem in dynamic modeling and high-speed control of fluidic prestressed composite mechanisms.
The lack of contact mechanics within the CCM reveals a need for integrating contact and distributed grasping models to predict multi-finger grasp stability and payload limits.
The absence of feedback sensing indicates an opportunity to explore embedded strain or tactile sensing within prestressed laminated composites for closed-loop shape and force control.
paper.research_objective: To develop and validate an analytical large-deflection model (chained composite model, CCM) for fluidic prestressed composite (FPC) actuators under pressure and external loads, provide systematic parametric design guidelines relating structural dimensions to curvature and flexural rigidity, and demonstrate their application in a soft robotic gripper.
paper.research_problem: Highly deformable fluidic prestressed composite actuators are difficult to model under large deflections and non-constant curvatures using existing analytical small-rotation models, while finite-element methods incur high computational cost and empirical models lack physical insight into multimaterial mechanics.
stiffness_mechanism: prestressed elastomeric matrix composite (EMC) layer creating precurvature and passive holding stiffness without energy input
anisotropic stiffness via 90-degree carbon fiber-reinforced elastomeric composite
3D-printed polypropylene constraining layer with stiffening ribs
transverse and longitudinal internal elastomeric ribs suppressing channel ballooning
pneumatic pressure modulation of structural flexural rigidity
paper.title: Modeling of Fluidic Prestressed Composite Actuators With Application to Soft Robotic Grippers
